text: Magnetic Field On-the-job relevance up front: managers, facilities engineers and product owners will be able to spot, diagnose and make informed trade-offs when magnetic fields affect equipment or personnel. Performance gap: the target learners can reason qualitatively about electricity but cannot reliably translate magnetic-field concepts into workplace decisions (how to measure risk, choose mitigation, communicate trade-offs to stakeholders, or specify instruments and controls). Audience profile: mid-career technical professionals with a Bachelor's degree, practical experience in engineering or operations, limited formal training in magnetism, constrained time (microlearning, 5–10 minute modules), and responsibility for operational decisions. Tasks this course must produce: 1) translate magnetism concepts into actionable checks and measurements on site; 2) pick and justify mitigation options for interference or safety; 3) communicate technical trade-offs to peers and managers; 4) choose appropriate measurement instruments and interpret their outputs. Analysis notes: start with a short, plain-language refresher, then move to applied scenarios, decision trees and job aids so learners can apply skills immediately. Design and development flag: where diagrams, interactive branching decision trees, simulated dashboards or measurement-data visualisations are needed, the blueprint flags them as required media rather than long prose. SME verification: all measurement procedures, recommended instruments and safety- related claims must be validated by a subject-matter expert before release. Audience: Intermediate learners with some practical experience who want to deepen their skills. Template: Non-Technical Chapters: 3

You are the shift lead. After a scheduled upgrade, a new drive motor sits 15 cm from a photoelectric sensor. The sensor’s signal now jitters, causing false rejects. Stopping the line costs throughput; running blind risks quality escapes. Maintenance can be onsite in 30 minutes. You must decide in five: pause for diagnostics or run a quick remote check and continue. Takeaway: a shared mental model and a short checklist cut the decision time without guesswork. Takeaway: Decide fast by linking a simple current–field model to a proximity check and a crisp ticket note. Core Concept: how current relates to a magnetic field Concept: imagine <jargon term="current">current</jargon> as water flow in a pipe. The moving charge makes a surrounding <jargon term="magnetic field">magnetic field</jargon>, like ripples around the pipe. Near the pipe, the ‘ripples’ are stronger; farther away, they fade. Where this analogy breaks: there is no literal fluid around the wire, nothing is dragged by a flow, and the field has direction in space that the water image does not capture. Use it to picture ‘near stronger, far weaker’ and that fields wrap around the path of current. Magnetic Field 24 / 55

You lead a small automation cell. A lab technician reports that a magnetic pick-and-place tool occasionally misaligns ferrous pins by a millimeter. You map the scene: the magnetic tip, the nearby optical encoder, and a steel bracket that might redirect fields. Decision: you temporarily reposition the encoder 2 cm away and run a 10‐minute throughput test. Consequence: misalignments drop to near-zero, cycle time holds, and you avoid a rushed shielding purchase. If the test had failed, your next branch would be: swap in a non‐ferromagnetic spacer, then trial a small, targeted shield only if errors persist. Takeaway: A quick qualitative read plus a reversible test often resolves the issue faster than jumping to shielding. Core concept Magnetic Field 42 / 55

Takeaway: A quick qualitative read plus a reversible test often resolves the issue faster than jumping to shielding. Core concept Magnetic Field 42 / 55

Concept: Field lines, poles, and attraction/repulsion Field lines are a visual tool: imagine threads showing where a small test magnet would point. Lines crowd where the field is stronger. They leave the north pole and enter the south pole of a bar magnet. Like poles repel; unlike poles attract. Ferromagnetic materials (for example, mild steel) give the field an easier path, so lines bend through them. This is why a steel bracket can channel a field toward a sensor, even if the magnet sits farther away. Field lines leave the north pole and enter the south pole; a steel bracket bends and concentrates lines toward a distant sensor. Magnetic Field 43 / 55

Flux: total field passing through an area. Permeability: how easily material lets field pass. Saturation: when material can’t carry more field and extra lines spill into air. Analogy limit: unlike water pipes, field “flow” has no conserved fluid; use lines only as a guide. Core concept: annotated field diagrams — bar magnet vs. current-carrying conductor. Magnetic Field 44 / 55

Workplace difference: a bar magnet’s lines arch from N to S, concentrating at poles and into nearby steel. A straight conductor’s field forms circles around the wire, strongest close-in, fading with distance. This matters when placing sensors: around magnets, avoid pole-facing directions and steel paths; around conductors, step sideways to exit the circular bands. When steel is present, watch for saturation—beyond that point, lines spill into air unpredictably.

text: Escalate beyond sketches when: safety margins are unclear, compliance limits are approached, simple measurements disagree beyond your tolerance, or remediation cost is high. Next steps: perform instrumented mapping, document uncertainties, request targeted modeling (for example, finite‐element analysis), and escalate to a subject‐matter expert for sign‐off. Have the escalation thresholds, instrument selection, and any references to compliance limits reviewed by a qualified magnetics SME before release. Real-world example A motor’s stray field disrupted a nearby magnetic encoder. The qualitative read: dense circular fields near phase conductors and a steel mount guiding lines toward the encoder. Actions: move the encoder laterally by a small offset, add a thin non‐ferromagnetic spacer, then test. Result: noise decreased. Only then add a small local shield to the bracket—not around the motor—to avoid airflow and maintenance issues. The sequence followed the field picture, not habit. Magnetic Field 45 / 55

Field shapes, steel effects (saturation), and practical sensor moves: step sideways near wires, avoid pole-facing/steel paths, then offset, spacer, and a small bracket shield in the motor example.

Repositioning stepped out of the circular field bands. The spacer broke a steel path. The shield targeted the path, not the source, reducing side effects.
